passages.source_text: πρὸς τούτοις δὲ τοῦ πατρὸς τὸ μὴ γεγεννῆσθαί ἐστιν, υἱοῦ δὲ τὸ γεγεννῆσθαι· γεννητὸν δὲ ἀγεννήτῳ ἢ καὶ αὐτογεννήτῳ οὐ συγκρίνεται. καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Εἰ καὶ τῇ γενέσει οὐ ταὐτόν ἐστιν; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Ὁ μὴ κατὰ πάντα τὸ αὐτὸ ὢν τινι τὰς αὐτὰς αὐτῷ πάσας ἔχειν προσωνυμίας οὐ δύναται. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Τοῦτο λέγειν ἐστίν, οὐκ ἀποδεικνύειν. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Διὰ τί οὐ νοεῖς ὅτι τὸ μὲν αὐτογέννητον τυγχάνει ἢ καὶ ἀγέννητον, τὸ δὲ γεννητὸν ὂν τὸ αὐτὸ λέγεσθαι οὐ δύναται, οὐδ᾽ ἂν τῆς αὐτῆς οὐσίας ὁ γεγεννημένος τῷ γεγεννηκότι .... ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῦτο μάθε· τὰ ἀνθρώπων σώματα ψυχὰς ἔχει ἀθανάτους, τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ πνοὴν ἠμφιεσμένας. καὶ ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ προελθοῦσαι τῆς μὲν αὐτῆς οὐσίας εἰσί, θεοὶ δὲ οὐκ εἰσίν. εἰ δὲ θεοί εἰσι, τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ πάντων ἀνθρώπων (τῶν τε ἀποθανόντων καὶ ζώντων καὶ γεννηθησομένων) αἱ ψυχαὶ θεοὶ τυγχάνουσιν. εἰ δὲ προσφιλονεικῶν μοι ἐρεῖς καὶ αὐτὰς θεοὺς εἶναι: καὶ τί τοῦτο ἔτι μέγα καὶ χριστῷ, τὸ θεῷ λέγεσθαι; τοῦτο γὰρ ἔχει, ὃ καὶ πάντες ἔχουσιν.

ἡμεῖς θεὸν λέγομεν, οὗ ἐστιν ἴδιον τὸ ἄλλῳ προσεῖναι μὴ δυνάμενον. ὥσπερ γὰρ ἄπειρος ὢν πανταχόθεν διὰ τοῦτο λέγεται ἀπέραντος, καὶ ἀνάγκη πᾶσα, ἑτέρου μὴ δυναμένου ὡσαύτως ἀπείρου εἶναι, μὴ εἶναι ἴδιον τὸ καλεῖσθαι ἀπέραντος (εἰ δέ τις λέγει δυνατὸν εἶναι, ψεύδεται· δύο γὰρ πανταχόθεν ἄπειρα συνυπάρχειν οὐ δύναται· περαιοῦται γὰρ τὸ ἕτερον ὑπὸ τοῦ ἑτέρου): οὕτως φύσις ἐστὶν ἓν εἶναι τὸ ἀγέννητον. εἰ δὲ ἐν σχήματί ἐστιν: καὶ οὕτως ἓν ἐστιν τὸ ἀσύγκριτον. διὰ τοῦτο καὶ ὕψιστος λέγεται, ὅτι πάντων ἀνώτερος ὢν τὰ πάντα αὐτῷ ὑποκείμενα ἔχει.

καὶ ὁ Σίμων Μὴ γὰρ τοῦτό ἐστιν αὐτοῦ ἀπόρρητον ὄνομα, τὸ „θεός“, ὅπερ πάντες λέγουσιν, ὅτι τοσοῦτον καὶ περὶ ὀνόματος διισχυρίζῃ, ἵνα μὴ ἄλλῳ δοθῇ; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος ἔφη Ἐπίσταμαι ὅτι τοῦτο οὐκ ἔστιν αὐτῷ τὸ ἀπόρρητον ὄνομα, ἀλλὰ τὸ κατὰ συνθήκην ἀνθρώπων λεγόμενον, ὅπερ εἰ ἑτέρῳ δώσεις, καὶ τὸ μὴ λεγόμενον ἑτέρῳ προσάψεις, καὶ τῷ τῆς προαιρέσεως λόγῳ τὸ λεγόμενον ὄνομα τοῦ μὴ λεγομένου πρόοδός ἐστιν. τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ ἡ ὕβρις καὶ εἰς τὸ μήπω ῥηθὲν λογίζεται, ᾧ λόγῳ ἡ πρὸς τὸ ἐγνωσμένον τιμὴ εἰς τὸ μήπω ἐγνωσμένον ἀναφέρεται.

καὶ ὁ Σίμων ἔφη Ἤθελον εἰδέναι, Πέτρε, εἰ ἀληθῶς πιστεύεις ὅτι ἡ ἀνθρώπου μορφὴ πρὸς τὴν ἐκείνου μορφὴν διατετύπωται. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Ἀληθῶς, ὦ Σίμων, οὕτως ἔχειν πεπληροφόρημαι. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Πῶς θάνατος τὸ σῶμα λύειν δύναται, σφραγῖδι μεγίστῃ διατετυπωμένον; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Θεοῦ δικαίου ἐστὶν μορφή. ἐπὰν οὖν ἀδικεῖν ἄρξηται, ἡ ἐν αὐτῷ ἰδέα φεύγει, καὶ οὕτως τὸ σῶμα λύεται, ἵνα ἡ μορφὴ ἀφανὴς γένηται, ὅπως μὴ δικαίου θεοῦ μορφὴν ἄδικον ἔχῃ σῶμα. ἡ μέντοι λύσις οὐ περὶ τὴν σφραγῖδα γίνεται, ἀλλὰ περὶ τὸ σφραγισθὲν σῶμα. ἄνευ δὲ τοῦ σφραγίσαντος τὸ σφραγισθὲν οὐ λύεται. οὕτως ἄνευ κρίσεως οὐδὲ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν ἔξεστιν. καὶ ὁ Σίμων Τίς οὖν ἀνάγκη ἦν τὴν τοιούτου μορφὴν τῷ ἀπὸ γῆς ἐγερθέντι δοῦναι ἀνθρώπῳ; καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Διὰ τὴν τοῦ πεποιηκότος θεοῦ φιλανθρωπίαν γέγονεν. ἐπεὶ γὰρ τῷ κατ’ οὐσίαν λόγῳ πάντα κρείττονα τυγχάνει τῆς ἀνθρώπου σαρκός, λέγω δὲ τὸν αἰθέρα, τὸν ἥλιον, τὴν σελήνην, τοὺς ἀστέρας, τὸν ἀέρα, τὸ ὕδωρ, τὸ πῦρ, ἑνὶ λόγῳ καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ πάντα, ἅτινα εἰς ὑπηρεσίαν ἀνθρώπου γενόμενά καὶ κατ’ οὐσίαν κρείττονα ὄντα ἡδέως ὑπομένει δουλεύειν τῷ κατ’ οὐσίαν χείρονι διὰ τὴν τοῦ κρείττονος μορφὴν (ὡς γὰρ οἱ πήλινον ἀνδριάντα βασιλέως τιμῶντες τὴν τιμὴν ἀναφερομένην ἔχουσιν εἰς ἐκεῖνον, οὗπερ ὁ πηλὸς τὴν μορφὴν τυγχάνει ἔχων, οὕτως καὶ ἡ πᾶσα κτίσις τῷ ἀπὸ γῆς γενομένῳ ἀνθρώπῳ χαίρουσα δουλεύει, εἰς τὴν ἐκείνου ἀφορῶσα τιμήν):

ἰδὲ οἵῳ θεῷ, Σίμων, ἀχαριστεῖν ἡμᾶς πεῖσαι θέλεις· καὶ βαστάζει σε ἡ γῆ, ἴσως δὲ ἰδεῖν βουλομένῃ τίς σοι τὰ ὅμοια φρονεῖν τολμήσοι. πρῶτος γὰρ ἐτόλμησας, ὃ μηδεὶς ἐτόλμησεν· πρῶτος ἐφθέγξω, ἃ πρώτως ἠκούσαμεν. πρῶτοι καὶ μόνοι ἡμεῖς ἐπὶ τοιαύτῃ σου ἀσεβείᾳ τὴν ἄπειρον τοῦ θεοῦ μακροθυμίαν ἱστορήσαμεν καὶ οὐκ ἄλλου τινὸς ἢ τοῦ κτίσαντος τὸν κόσμον, εἰς ὃν ἀσεβεῖν ἐτόλμησας. καὶ χάσματα γῆς οὐκ ἐγενήθη καὶ πῦρ ἀπ’ οὐρανοῦ οὐ κατεπέμφθη καὶ εἰς ἐμπρησμὸν ἀνδρῶν οὐκ ἐπεξῆλθεν, καὶ ὑετὸς οὐκ ἐπεσχέθη καὶ θηρῶν πλῆθος ἀπὸ δρυμῶν οὐκ ἐπέμφθη, καὶ ἐπ’ αὐτοὺς ἡμᾶς διὰ ἕνα ἁμαρτάνοντα ὡς ἐπὶ μοιχείας πνευματικῆς τῆς κατὰ σάρκα χείρονος ὑπαρχούσης ἡ θεοῦ ὀργὴ ὀλέθριος οὐκ ἤρξατο. οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν ὁ τότε ἐπεξελθὼν τὰ ἁμαρτήματα οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς κτίστης θεός; ἐπεὶ καὶ νῦν τὰ μέγιστα βλασφημούμενος τὰ μέγιστα ἐπεξήρχετο. ἀλλὰ τοὐναντίον μακροθυμεῖ, εἰς μετάνοιαν καλεῖ, συντελοῦντα βέλη πρὸς συντέλειαν τῶν ἀσεβῶν ἐν τοῖς θησαυροῖς ἀποκείμενα ἔχων, ἅτινα ἐπαφήσει ὡς ζῷα ἔμψυχα, ὅταν ἀνταποδοῦναι κρίσιν τοῖς ἐχθροῖς αὐτοῦ προκαθεσθῇ. διὸ φοβηθῶμεν θεὸν δίκαιον, οὗ τὴν μορφὴν πρὸς τιμὴν τὸ ἀνθρώπου βαστάζει σῶμα.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: ‘Besides, it belongs to the Father not to have been begotten, but to the Son to have been begotten. What is begotten is not comparable with what is unbegotten or even self-begotten.’ Simon said, ‘Even if it is the same in respect of generation?’ Peter said, ‘One who is not in every respect the same as another cannot have all the same designations as that one.’ Simon said, ‘That is assertion, not demonstration.’ Peter said, ‘Why do you not understand that the one is self-begotten or even unbegotten, whereas the other, being begotten, cannot be called the same, not even if the begotten one is of the same substance as the begetter .... But learn this too: human bodies have immortal souls clothed in God's breath. Having come forth from God, they are of the same substance, but are not gods. If they are gods, then by that reasoning the souls of all humans—those who have died, those living, and those yet to be born—are gods. But if, persisting in your argument with me, you say that they too are gods, what great distinction remains even for the Messiah in being called God? For he has what everyone also has.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γεννητὸν δὲ ἀγεννήτῳ ἢ καὶ αὐτογεννήτῳ οὐ συγκρίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: What is begotten is not comparable with what is unbegotten or even self-begotten
lexical_decisions.rationale: The three generation terms and their distinctions are retained. Self-begotten is not silently collapsed into unbegotten, and the comparison is not rewritten to assert a later creedal formula.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Εἰ καὶ τῇ γενέσει οὐ ταὐτόν ἐστιν;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Even if it is the same in respect of generation?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The interrogative negative is read as seeking the admission that it is the same in respect of generation. More literally, Even if, in generation, is it not the same? Generation can mean coming-to-be or birth; the subsequent substance argument supplies context but does not erase the term.

The phrase is retained both in the conditional argument about the begotten one and the subsequent account of souls. The passage's own distinction between shared substance and the title God is not harmonized with another theological position.

The supplied dative form occurs in the title-ascription expression. The English preserves the intended naming construction without supplying a further predicate or claiming to correct the printed Greek.

source_issues.issue: The edition prints four dots after the begetter clause. The English preserves exactly four dots, without supplying a missing verb or continuation. Its rendering of is in the preceding conditional clause provides ordinary English copular syntax and does not claim to restore the unavailable wording after the clause.

passages.text: ‘We call God the one whose distinctive property cannot belong to another. For just as he is called boundless because he is infinite in every direction, and it is altogether necessary, since another cannot likewise be infinite, that being called boundless not be a property of another—if anyone says this is possible, he lies, for two things infinite in every direction cannot coexist, since each is bounded by the other—so it is natural for the unbegotten to be one. Even if he has a shape, in this way too the incomparable is one. For this reason he is also called Most High, because, being above all, he has everything subject to himself.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μὴ εἶναι ἴδιον τὸ καλεῖσθαι ἀπέραντος
lexical_decisions.chosen: that being called boundless not be a property of another
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative is retained, and of another is inferred from the immediately preceding statement that another cannot likewise be infinite. If distinctive property is instead attached to God without that contextual complement, the clause appears to deny the distinctiveness it argues for. The main reading preserves the negation and supplies the contextually available referent, not a conjectural alteration of the Greek.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Even if he has a shape
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional concession is retained. The phrase does not deny shape in order to impose a different doctrine of divine incorporeality.
The superlative title is translated and immediately explained by the source's claim of superiority over all.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘Surely “God,” which everyone says, is not his unutterable name, that you insist so strongly even about the name, so that it may not be given to another?’ Peter said, ‘I know that this is not his unutterable name, but the one spoken by human convention. If you give this to another, you will attach the unspoken one to another too. In terms of intention, the spoken name is an advance toward the unspoken one. On this account the insult is reckoned also against what has not yet been spoken, just as honor directed toward what is known is referred to what is not yet known.’

lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can denote a name not to be divulged or spoken. Secret name is another possible emphasis; the subsequent spoken/unspoken contrast supports unutterable without specifying the hidden name's letters.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ λεγόμενον ὄνομα τοῦ μὴ λεγομένου πρόοδός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the spoken name is an advance toward the unspoken one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The movement metaphor is retained. In terms of intention qualifies how assigning the public title implicates the unnamed divine identity; no separate name or magical utterance is supplied.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘I wished to know, Peter, whether you truly believe that the human form has been patterned after his form.’ Peter said, ‘Truly, Simon, I am fully convinced that this is so.’ Simon said, ‘How can death dissolve the body when it is patterned by the greatest seal?’ Peter said, ‘It is the form of a righteous God. When it begins to do wrong, the image within it flees, and so the body dissolves, in order that the form may disappear and an unrighteous body may not possess the form of a righteous God. The dissolution, however, concerns not the seal but the body that was sealed. The sealed thing is not dissolved without the one who sealed it. Thus it is not permitted even to die without judgment.’ Simon said, ‘What need was there, then, to give the form of such a one to the human raised from the earth?’ Peter said, ‘This happened because of the creating God's love for humanity. For in respect of substance everything is superior to human flesh—I mean the ether, the sun, the moon, the stars, air, water, fire, in a word, everything else too. These things, having come into being for human service and being superior in substance, gladly endure serving what is inferior in substance because of the form of the superior one. For just as those honoring a clay statue of a king have their honor referred to the one whose form the clay bears, so all creation gladly serves the human made from earth, looking toward that one's honor.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὰν οὖν ἀδικεῖν ἄρξηται, ἡ ἐν αὐτῷ ἰδέα φεύγει
lexical_decisions.chosen: When it begins to do wrong, the image within it flees
lexical_decisions.rationale: It refers to the body or embodied person under discussion. The distinction between the departing image and the dissolving sealed body is maintained, rather than replacing image with a named material organ.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄνευ δὲ τοῦ σφραγίσαντος τὸ σφραγισθὲν οὐ λύεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: The sealed thing is not dissolved without the one who sealed it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase does not explicitly name permission, presence, or action as the sense of without. The English leaves that relation broad; without the sealer's permission is a contextual explanatory alternative but adds an unexpressed noun.
The comparison concerns what things consist of, not their moral worth. Its repetition distinguishes superior substance from the honor attached to the inferior human body's divine form.

The king-statue comparison points to the superior original whose form the human bears. That one preserves the pronoun while the note identifies its contextual direction; it does not claim that earth itself is the king.

passages.text: ‘See, Simon, what kind of God you wish to persuade us to be ungrateful toward! The earth still carries you, perhaps wishing to see who would dare to think as you do. For you were the first to dare what no one had dared, the first to utter what we heard for the first time. We were the first and only ones to witness God's boundless patience in the face of such impiety from you—not that of some other god, but of the one who created the world, against whom you dared to be impious. No chasms opened in the earth, no fire was sent down from heaven or advanced to burn people, no rain was withheld, no multitude of wild beasts was sent from the thickets, and God's destructive wrath did not begin even against us because of one sinner, as in the case of spiritual adultery, which is worse than adultery according to the flesh. For is not the one who then punished sins the God who created heaven and earth? For even now, most grievously blasphemed, he would have inflicted the greatest punishment. But, on the contrary, he is patient and calls us to reorientation toward God. He has destructive arrows stored in his treasuries for the destruction of the impious, which he will release like living creatures when he takes his seat to repay his enemies with judgment. Therefore let us fear the righteous God whose form the human body bears as an honor.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἴσως δὲ ἰδεῖν βουλομένῃ τίς σοι τὰ ὅμοια φρονεῖν τολμήσοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: perhaps wishing to see who would dare to think as you do
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine participle is read as continuing the personified earth, despite its oblique inflection beside the nominative earth. Perhaps qualifies the conjecture; the English does not replace the earth with an unexpressed masculine observer.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν ὁ τότε ἐπεξελθὼν τὰ ἁμαρτήματα οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς κτίστης θεός;
lexical_decisions.chosen: For is not the one who then punished sins the God who created heaven and earth?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed negative question is retained rather than turned into a categorical identification or categorical denial. Its relation to the following counterfactual punishment and contrasting patience is rhetorically difficult. A reading that challenges the attribution of the earlier punishments to the creator is materially possible; the main text preserves the question rather than deleting the negative or resolving the theology by emendation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: calls us to reorientation toward God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied English policy uses reorientation for moral-spiritual redirection, with toward God where the context supports the destination. Here the creator's invitation contrasts with the preceding impiety against him; us is the contextually inferred addressee, not a claim that God himself must reorient.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: συντελοῦντα βέλη πρὸς συντέλειαν τῶν ἀσεβῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: destructive arrows ... for the destruction of the impious
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated completion or ending root describes final, destructive force. The English retains the destructive aim and the arrows image without supplying a specific weapon technology.
The life-bearing comparison is explicit; it does not say that the arrows are literally a named species of animal or angel.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
